content.title: About
content.content: Canned carrots cooked in vegetable oil are peeled, sliced, blanched and then sealed in a jar with added oil. The product is ready to eat, retaining a bright orange colour, soft texture and a mildly sweet flavour.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Canned carrots are often used as an ingredient in salads, side dishes and cold appetizers.
The oil in the jar helps retain moisture and enhances the taste.
Carrots are rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Canning allows storage for up to 2‑3 years at room temperature.
In some countries carrots are canned in olive oil, giving them a Mediterranean aroma.

items.title: Rich source of vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene from carrots is converted into vitamin A, essential for vision, immunity and skin health.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Carotenoids and vitamin C protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Dietary fibre in carrots promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Provides potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and blood pressure.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: A 100 g serving contains about 80 kcal, making it suitable for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Oil content
items.content: The product contains vegetable oil, so those monitoring fat intake should consider its calories.

items.title: Salt and preservatives
items.content: Some varieties add salt or preservatives; people with hypertension or sensitivities should check the label.

items.title: Carrot allergy
items.content: Rare, but an allergic reaction to carrots is possible.

items.title: Can integrity
items.content: If the lid is damaged or the jar is bulging, the product may be spoiled and pose a food‑borne illness risk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned carrots can be eaten straight from the jar, added to salads, stews, pasta, omelets, or used as a side dish for meat and fish. They can also be gently warmed in a pan if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep refrigerated in a sealed container for no more than 5‑7 days. Discard if an off‑odor or discoloration appears.

content.title: About
content.content: Reduced‑fat Muenster cheese is a semi‑hard cheese made from cow’s milk, traditionally produced in the Münster region of Germany. The lower fat content makes it lighter while preserving its characteristic mild, nutty aroma and slightly sweet taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Muenster cheese gets its name from the city of Münster, where it was first produced in the 17th century.
Traditional Muenster is aged 4–6 weeks; the reduced‑fat version is aged a bit shorter to keep a tender texture.
The cheese melts well, making it popular for grilled sandwiches and casseroles.
Fat reduction is achieved by partially skimming the milk and adding low‑fat curd.
Muenster is often served in slices with fruit, bread, or melted over hot dishes.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Muenster provides about 25 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Approximately 500 mg of calcium per 100 g helps strengthen bones and teeth.

items.title: Reduced fat
items.content: With fat content around 10 %, it fits better into lower‑calorie diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Probiotic cultures
items.content: Fermentation leaves live bacteria that may support gut health.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Residual lactose can cause discomfort for those who are lactose intolerant.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to casein, the main milk protein.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The cheese is moderately salty; people monitoring sodium intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Despite reduced fat, it still provides about 250 kcal per 100 g.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Reduced‑fat Muenster works well in sandwiches, melted in casseroles, grated over salads, or served with fresh fruit. Slice thinly or shred as needed.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cheese in its original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C. Once opened, consume within 2‑3 weeks. Discard if mold develops or the cheese develops an off‑odor.

content.title: About
content.content: Iced Coffee, pre-lightened and pre-sweetened (5183) is a ready‑to‑drink cold coffee that has been lightly roasted and sweetened. It offers a smooth roasted aroma, gentle sweetness, and a refreshing texture, perfect for quick consumption without adding extra sugar or milk.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cold coffee retains most of the antioxidants found in hot brewed coffee.
Pre‑lightening reduces bitterness, giving the beverage a milder flavor.
Sweetening is usually done with natural sweeteners such as sucrose or fructose.
While often served over ice, it can also be used as a base for cocktails and desserts.
The product has a long shelf life thanks to its airtight packaging.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Coffee contains polyphenols that help combat free radicals and support cellular health.

items.title: Boosts alertness
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, improving concentration and reaction time.

items.title: Supports metabolism
items.content: Caffeine may increase metabolic rate, aiding calorie burning.

items.title: Improves mood
items.content: Caffeine promotes the release of dopamine and serotonin, which can enhance mood.

items.title: Contributes to hydration
items.content: Although coffee has a mild diuretic effect, in moderate amounts it adds to daily fluid intake.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience anxiety, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat after caffeine consumption.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweetened coffee can raise blood glucose levels, especially for people with diabetes.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Coffee’s acidity may irritate the stomach in those with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Coffee allergy
items.content: Rarely, an allergic reaction to coffee components can occur.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink the iced coffee straight from the bottle, add ice, milk, cream, or flavored syrups to taste. It can also serve as a base for frappés, smoothies, dessert sauces, and marinades.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, keep refrigerated and consume within 2–3 days.

popcorn-popped-in-oil-with-added-butter.title: Popcorn, popped in oil with added butter

content.title: About
content.content: Popcorn is made from corn kernels that explode when heated, creating light, airy pieces. In this version the kernels are popped in vegetable oil and then tossed with butter, giving a rich, buttery flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Popcorn is one of the oldest snacks, enjoyed by ancient Mexican and Peruvian cultures.
Each kernel contains about 14 % water; when heated the water turns to steam and forces the kernel to pop.
Butter enhances flavor perception by increasing the sensitivity of taste buds to salty and sweet notes.
While popcorn is a staple in movie theaters, the home‑made version lets you control salt and fat levels.
There are over 30 corn varieties suitable for popping; only specific “pop‑corn” types give consistent results.

items.title: Relatively low in calories compared with other snacks
items.content: Popcorn provides about 380 kcal per 100 g, but its low density means you can eat a large volume without excessive calories.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports healthy digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Polysaccharides and polyphenols in corn have antioxidant properties that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Popcorn provides thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Heart‑friendly when prepared with healthy oil
items.content: Moderate consumption of oil‑popped popcorn can help lower LDL cholesterol thanks to its polyunsaturated fat content.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Adding butter raises the calorie count and saturated fat levels; people watching weight or cholesterol should limit portions.

items.title: Milk allergy
items.content: Butter may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with dairy protein intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Burn risk
items.content: Hot popcorn can burn the mouth and esophagus; let it cool slightly before eating.

items.title: Salt and additives
items.content: Excessive salt increases the risk of hypertension; choose a lightly salted version when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Popcorn is perfect as a stand‑alone snack, during movie nights, as a base for sweet or savory mixes, and can be flavored with spices such as paprika, garlic powder, or cheese seasoning.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store popcorn in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life keep it in the refrigerator to prevent oil from going rancid. Discard popcorn that becomes soft, develops an off‑odor, or changes color.

pretzels-soft-gluten-free-coated-or-flav.title: Soft Gluten-Free Pretzels, Coated or Flavored

content.title: About
content.content: Soft gluten‑free pretzels are baked from gluten‑free grains such as rice, corn or buckwheat, combined with starch and a small amount of yeast. They can be coated with salt, cheese, spices or sweet glazes. The pretzels have a tender crumb, a light aroma and are suitable for people with gluten intolerance.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Gluten‑free pretzels are a popular snack for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.
Traditional German pretzels are knotted and crunchy, while the soft versions are usually flat and pliable.
Coatings may include sea salt, cheese powder, spicy blends, cinnamon‑sugar, or chocolate glaze.
Using gluten‑free flours allows the pretzel to keep a crisp exterior with a soft interior.
The U.S. gluten‑free snack market is growing at over 12 % annually.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Most varieties contain little to no added sugar, making them suitable for moderate consumption.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Gluten‑free grains provide slow‑releasing energy.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Rice and corn flours supply niacin, thiamine and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Completely safe for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Grain allergies
items.content: Some gluten‑free blends may contain soy protein or dairy, which can trigger allergies.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Salted versions can be high in sodium; choose unsalted or lightly salted if you have hypertension.

items.title: Additive content
items.content: Glazes and flavorings may include artificial sweeteners or preservatives.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Despite being gluten‑free, pretzels are still calorie‑dense due to starch and coating fats.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy pretzels as a snack on their own, pair with dips (hummus, yogurt sauce), add to salads, or use in appetizer platters. Sweet‑coated pretzels pair well with coffee or tea.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer shelf life keep them in the refrigerator to maintain crispness. Avoid moisture, which can make pretzels soggy.

salami-sandwich-on-white-with-cheese.title: Salami sandwich on white, with cheese

content.title: About
content.content: A salami sandwich on white bread with cheese is a popular quick snack consisting of a slice of white roll, thinly sliced salami and melted or firm cheese. The salami adds a spicy, slightly smoky flavor, while the cheese provides a creamy texture and enhances the aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Salami originated in Italy in the 19th century as a method of preserving meat.
White bread is often used for sandwiches because its soft crumb does not overpower the filling.
The combination of salty salami and creamy cheese is considered a classic in European street food.
In some countries the sandwich is served warm, lightly toasted so the cheese melts.
Salami can be made from pork, beef, or a mixture of both.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Both salami and cheese are rich in animal protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Red meat in salami provides heme iron, which is more readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese is a good source of calcium, supporting bone and tooth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat products supply vitamin B12 and niacin, important for the nervous system and metabolism.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The sandwich quickly replenishes energy stores thanks to a balance of carbs, fats and proteins.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Salami and many cheeses contain a lot of salt, which can raise blood pressure if eaten frequently.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Salami and firm cheese are high in saturated fats, which should be limited in heart‑related conditions.

items.title: Preservatives and nitrites
items.content: Some salami varieties use nitrites, which may be harmful in large amounts.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein should avoid the cheese component.

items.title: Gluten in bread
items.content: White bread contains gluten, making it unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is usually served cold, but it can be lightly toasted in a pan or grill to melt the cheese. Adding lettuce, tomato slices or mustard can add extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the assembled sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours. Store salami and cheese separately in their original packaging, and keep the bread in a dry place to prevent it from becoming stale.

sausage-and-rice-with-cheese-sauce.title: Sausage and Rice with Cheese Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Sausage and rice with cheese sauce is a ready‑to‑eat dish consisting of boiled rice, pieces of cooked or smoked sausage, and a creamy cheese‑based sauce. It is commonly served hot in cafeterias, cafés, and as a pre‑packaged meal in supermarkets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish combines protein from meat with carbohydrates from rice, providing a quick energy source.
The cheese sauce is often made from processed cheese, giving it a smooth texture and mild flavor.
Some regional recipes add spices such as paprika, black pepper, or dried garlic for extra aroma.
It can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 3 days and reheated in a microwave.
Using whole‑grain rice increases the fiber content.

items.title: Protein from sausage
items.content: Sausage supplies essential amino acids that support tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Energy‑rich rice
items.content: Rice provides complex carbohydrates that release energy gradually.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: The cheese sauce contributes calcium, important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and rice are good sources of B1, B2, and B6 vitamins, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The combination of protein, fat, and carbs helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Processed sausages often contain a lot of salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Both the cheese sauce and sausage can be high in saturated fats, which should be limited in heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some sausages contain nitrites and other preservatives that can cause allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish is relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the dish in a microwave or skillet until it reaches 75 °C. Serve hot, optionally garnished with fresh herbs, chopped green onions, or grated cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0–4 °C in an airtight container for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze for up to 2 months; fully thaw and reheat before consumption.
